I don't know when the particular phrase was first used, but the idea is common in 19th century American literature, and in European literature back to the 17th century. It isn't even a modern idea, the same sentiments were expressed by ancient Greek philosophers regarding some barbarians. On the blankets, there are several 18th century letters extant that indicate the use of infected blankets as a means to "send the Small Pox among those disaffected tribes of Indians...You will do well to try to inoculate the Indians by means of blankets, as well as to try every other method that can serve to extirpate this execrable race." Nowadays we nearly always the word "inoculate" in a very strict way - that of introducing an antigenic substance into a body in order to produce antibodies, i.e. disease prevention. But the meaning of the word is simply to communicate or pass on a disease, without a specific intention. In the case of the quote above the intention is clear: "to extirpate this execrable race."
